parsed.attack: The pain named - 'not having something specific to say on the phone' - is an author's inference, not a complaint anyone makes; what grandparents actually report wanting is more contact, and what they do about it is call. The whole value chain hangs on the parents, who are the exhausted, non-paying, non-benefiting party, continuing to share photographs weekly forever - and their failure to do so is the root cause of the disconnection in the first place, which is why the author's own kill criterion anticipates households dropping below five photos by week six. Gift subscriptions to the over-70s have famously poor renewal because the person who feels the value is not the person holding the card, and the recipient cohort is the hardest population in consumer software to hold across four consecutive weekly opens. The cited evidence is two dead products; nothing here records a grandparent or a parent asking for a weekly written briefing.
parsed.strongest_defence: The wedge explicitly uses photographs the parents already shared this week, so it requires no new behaviour from the middle party at all - it is a passive read of an existing family album or chat - and the recipient does not need an app: one page at a fixed hour is the format this cohort has reliably consumed their whole lives.
parsed.verdict_reason: The felt pain is contact rather than conversational material, and the product depends on sustained supply from the one party who gets nothing from it, though passive ingestion of an existing album blunts the worst of it.
